A dance that never stops — stopped

Describe

Look at the bodies, the gown, the light and the crop. Follow the line of the dress: where does it go, and where does it stop?

Production

This is a studio publicity photograph from 1935, not a frame of the film. Who posed it, and for whom?

Critical

She leans back and he holds her. What does the photograph freeze that the dance itself would never stop on?

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

1 · The cloth arrives after the body

When a dancer moves, the fabric follows a moment later — and as we watch, we feel that movement in our own body.

we map these postures and gestures onto our own body, feeling them in our own skin and bones

(Shinkle 2008, 222)

Very little film of Isadora Duncan dancing is known: her dance reaches us mostly through photographs.

Image: Isadora Duncan, barefoot, in a loose tunic, one arm raised against a dark ground.

Isadora Duncan dancing LOC agc.7a09881 · Arnold Genthe · Public domain · Source

  • Play the Muybridge loop in the lesson: the hem lands after the step.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

2 · Two artists borrow ancient Greece

Isadora Duncan danced in loose “Greek” tunics, and the designer Mariano Fortuny, born in Granada, pleated silk into a column he called Delphos.

This Delphos gown is in the Museo del Traje in Madrid. Whose “classical” body becomes the ideal — and who is left out?

Image: A long black finely pleated silk Delphos gown on a mannequin.

Museo del Traje - MT111885 - Vestido Delphos · Museo del Traje (photograph); Mariano Fortuny y Madrazo (gown) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Source

  • Drape: the garment follows and lengthens the gesture.
  • A revival is not the ancient practice itself.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

3 · A patent for flying cloth

In 1894 the dancer Loïe Fuller patented a “garment for dancers”: a huge skirt hung from the head and thrown into waves with light wands.

Open Fuller's 1894 patent

Toulouse-Lautrec painted her in Paris in 1893 as swirling colour: the cloth, not the body.

Image: Loose painted sketch: a figure almost disappears inside green, white and violet swirls of cloth.

(Albi) - La Loïe Fuller aux-Folies-Bergère - Toulouse-Lautrec (1893) MTL.152 · Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec · Public domain · Source

  • Extension: the costume becomes the image.
  • Who gets the credit: dancer, maker, or the person who filed the patent?

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

4 · Many films called “Loïe Fuller” show someone else

Fuller's serpentine dance was copied everywhere, so early films sold under her name often show other dancers. Every old film is evidence to check.

Play the three serpentine films in the lesson

Image: A dancer outdoors swings a long sheer scarf in a wide arc above her head.

Loie Fuller dancing with scarf · Unknown photographer · Public domain · Source

  • Edison filmed Annabelle Whitford (1894); Lumière's dancer is unnamed (1897); a Pathé copy was hand-coloured by Segundo de Chomón in Barcelona.
  • The Pathé card says 1902, Commons says 1901: dates disagree.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

5 · A dancing body draws lines

The painter Wassily Kandinsky taught his Bauhaus students to look at a dancing body as a drawing made of lines.

The entire body of the dancer, right down to his finger tips, is at every moment an uninterrupted composition of lines

(Kandinsky 2012, “Line”)

Image: Three of Isadora Duncan’s dancers in tunics hold a veil above a seated figure.

Isadora Duncan dancers LOC agc.7a10003 · Arnold Genthe · Public domain · Source

  • Kandinsky credits the observation to the dancer Gret Palucca.
  • Trace one line in the image before speaking.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

6 · Start from one step

Oskar Schlemmer, who designed the Triadic Ballet in 1922, did not start from geometry. He started from a body standing on a stage.

Puesto que dar un paso es un acontecimiento grandioso, mientras que levantar una mano, mover un dedo, no lo son menos.

(Schlemmer 1987, 112)

In English: taking a step is a grand event — and raising a hand or moving a finger no less.

Image: Printed programme of the Triadic Ballet premiere listing twelve dances in yellow, pink and black series.

Das Triadische Ballett, Programmzettel 1922 · Oskar Schlemmer · Public domain · Source

  • A document, not a photograph of the premiere.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

7 · Geometry decides the step

Schlemmer's rigid costumes of cones, discs and spirals made some steps impossible and invented new ones.

Image: Triadic Ballet figures on a tiled stage: a spiked conical skirt, a club-like arm, a ballooning dark form.

Oskar Schlemmer Triadisches Ballett 200 · Oskar Schlemmer (figures); photographer not identified · Public domain · Source

  • Reorganisation: the costume writes the choreography.
  • Lab prompt C4 builds one of these in five minutes.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

8 · Four things a garment can do

A garment can do four things to a moving body: drape it, extend it, hold it in tension, or reorganise it completely.

Image: Museum display of three Triadic Ballet figures on low plinths against dark walls.

Triadisches Ballett by Oskar Schlemmer - Staatsgalerie - Stuttgart - Germany 2017 · José Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro (photograph); Oskar Schlemmer (figures) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Source

  • A museum display is not a performance.

What does the garment do to movement?

  • Place each clip and image on the map; defend the place with one frame.
  • A course hypothesis, not a fact.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

9 · The body pushes against the cloth

In Martha Graham's solo Lamentation, the dancer sits inside a tube of stretched jersey, and grief becomes visible as tension in the fabric.

Watch Graham's Night Journey in the lesson

Image: A seated dancer wrapped in a stretched tube of pale fabric; only face, hands and feet show.

Janet Eilber Performing Martha Graham’s “Lamentation” in the East Room of the White House - NARA - 30805967 · White House photographer (US National Archives) · Rights under review · Source

  • Tension: the garment resists and the body works against it.

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

10 · Same dance, different film

A camera chooses how close to stand and when to cut — and those choices decide whether we ever see the whole dress move.

Cameras will, with all their complex technical possibilities, in most cases still cling to and follow concrete body movements.

(Pfeiffer 2009, 198)

Image: Rogers in a full ruffled gown and Astaire in tails dance; her skirt flares wide.

Swing Time (1936) · RKO Radio Pictures (studio publicity photograph) · Public domain · Source

  • Play Cheek to Cheek from a licensed copy: count the cuts; check feet and hem.

Same dance, different film

  • Then play the Pina trailer in the lesson: where does Wim Wenders' camera stand?

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

11 · The public makes the star

Hollywood studios used fashion photographs to turn dancing stars into style models that audiences wanted to copy.

it's the public who makes the star

(Sill 2008, 127)

Image: Rogers mid-step in a light gown beside Astaire in tails on a shiny dance floor.

Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire - Follow the Fleet (1936) · RKO Radio Pictures (studio publicity photograph) · Public domain · Source

  • Who is credited: the dancers, the costume designer, the photographer?

Dance, cinema and fashion · Part 1 of 2

12 · When the stage met cinema

When film arrived, theatre could compete with it or learn from it. The Spanish film pioneer Segundo de Chomón turned the serpentine dance into special effects.

a theatre which, instead of competing against the newer means of communication, tries to apply them and to learn from them

(Benjamin 1998, 99)

Play Chomón's film of 1908 in the lesson

Image: A Muybridge frame: a woman in a light dress dancing before a gridded wall.

Eadweard Muybridge, Animal Locomotion, Woman Dancing (fancy), 1887, plate 187 · Eadweard Muybridge · Public domain · Source

  • Chomón: born Teruel 1871, died Paris 1929.
  • Your phone camera is today's version of this dialogue.

Recall check

Alone, from memory, three minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. What four things can a garment do to a moving body?
  2. Why should we doubt early films sold as “Loïe Fuller”?
  3. What does a full-figure shot show that a close-up hides?
  4. Who patented a “garment for dancers” in 1894?
  5. Who wrote that taking a step is a grand event?

Course geometric background · threshold · #c378606cc29b · Original course SVG

Answers:

  • Drape, extension, tension, reorganisation.
  • The dance was copied: other dancers appear under her name.
  • The feet, the hem, the whole garment in motion.
  • Loïe Fuller.
  • Oskar Schlemmer.

Exercise 1 · Capture movement with your phone

Choose two: a slow-motion spin, a burst of one turn, one take against three cuts, a stiff costume you build, or lines of light in a long exposure.

Peso, espacio, tiempo, y flujo.

(Laban 1987, 28)

All five prompts in the lesson

Keep your best capture and write one sentence: did the garment change the weight, the space, the time or the flow of the movement?
